newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler to move Asia unit to Singapore.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler to move Asia unit to Singapore.

text.p: Chrysler Corp., moving to boost its presence in Asia, on Friday said it would move its Asia/Pacific operations this summer to Singapore from outside Detroit.

Chrysler spokesman Michael Aberlich said Chrysler would shift about 20 managers from its current Asia/Pacific operations office at its Auburn Hills, Mich., headquarters to the new Singapore office, which will direct all sales, manufacturing and joint venture activities in the region.
The move is strategically similar to Chrysler's establishment of a European headquarters in Brussels in 1995.
"Instead of supporting our Chinese and Japanese operations out of Auburn Hills, we'll be supporting them out of Singapore," Aberlich said.

The Asia-Pacific operations also will maintain a northern Asia sub-regional office in Tokyo, which will coordinate activities in China, Japan, Korea and Taiwan. A southern Asia sub-regional office at the Singapore headquarters will oversee activities in southeast Asia, Indonesia, Australia and other areas.

Chrysler has been more cautious than General Motors Corp and Ford Motor Co about investing in assembly plants in Asia. Both GM and Ford are building full-scale assembly plants in Thailand and have signed production joint ventures in China.

Chrysler, which backed away from a minivan joint venture in China in late 1994 and more recently dropped plans to build a plant in Vietnam, said it was still actively seeking manufacturing joint ventures in the region.
"This (office) will make it easier for us to do that," Aberlich said.

The Auburn Hills-based group that oversees Chrysler's Asia/Pacific operations has about 60 people, about 40 of which are expected eventually to be reassigned, retire or leave the company, Aberlich said.
The Singapore office will maintain a staff of about 70, with about 50 people hired locally and from other Asian countries.

In other international activities Friday, Chrysler dedicated a small assembly plant in Cordoba, Argentina, which will build Jeep Grand Cherokee sport/utility vehicles for sale in the Mercosur trading group of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay.
The $165 million plant will have a production capacity of only 20,000 vehicles per year, with output of 2,500 units planned for 1997 and 10,000 for 1998.

"We anticipate strong demand for Jeep vehicles in Argentina and throughout the Mercosur, where the 4x4 segment is growing at a rapid rate, Chrysler Argentina's managing director, Charles Bush, said in a stateement. "By producing vehicles in-market, we can satisfy that demand more effectively."
